verses.zh: 那时，底波拉和亚比挪庵的儿子巴拉作歌，说：
verses.en: On that day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang this victory song:[NOTE:1]
notes: The words “this victory song” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

verses.zh: 因为以色列中有军长率领，百姓也甘心牺牲自己，你们应当颂赞耶和华！
verses.en: “When the leaders took the lead[NOTE:1] in Israel,When the people answered the call to war—Praise the Lord!
notes: The meaning of the Hebrew expression בִּפְרֹעַ פְּרָעוֹת (bifroaʿ peraʿot) is uncertain. Numerous proposals are offered by commentators. (For a survey of opinions, see B. Lindars, Judges 1-5, 223-27.) The next line refers to the people who responded to Barak’s summons to war, so a reference to the leaders who issued the summons would provide a natural poetic parallel. In v. 9 the leaders (חוֹקְקֵי, khoqeqe) of the people and these same volunteers stand in poetic parallelism, so it is reasonable to assume that the difficult Hebrew term פְּרַעוֹת (peraʿot, v. 2a) is synonymous with חוֹקְקֵי (khoqeqe) of v. 9 (see Lindars, 227).

verses.zh: 君王啊，要听！王子啊，要侧耳而听！我要向耶和华歌唱；我要歌颂耶和华―以色列的　神。
verses.en: Hear, O kings!Pay attention, O rulers!I will sing to the Lord![NOTE:1] I will sing[NOTE:2] to the Lord God of Israel!
notes: Heb “I, to the Lord, I, I will sing!” The first singular personal pronoun is used twice, even though a first person finite verbal form is employed.
Or “make music.”

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，你从西珥出来，由以东地行走。那时地震天漏，云也落雨。
verses.en: “O Lord, when you departed[NOTE:1] from Seir,when you marched from Edom’s plains,the earth shook, the heavens poured down,the clouds poured down rain.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “went out.”
Heb “water.”

verses.zh: 山见耶和华的面就震动，西奈山见耶和华―以色列　神的面也是如此。
verses.en: The mountains trembled[NOTE:1] before the Lord, the God of Sinai;[NOTE:2] before the Lord God of Israel.
notes: Or “quaked.” The translation assumes the form נָזֹלּוּ (nazollu) from the root זָלַל (zalal, “to quake”; see HALOT 272 s.v. II זלל). The LXX, the Syriac Peshitta, and the Targum also understood the word this way. (See Isa 63:19 and 64:2 for other occurrences of this form.) Some understand here the verb נָזַל (nazal, “to flow [with torrents of rain water]”).
Heb “this one of Sinai.” The phrase is a divine title, perhaps indicating that the Lord rules from Sinai.

verses.zh: 在亚拿之子珊迦的时候，又在雅亿的日子，大道无人行走，都是绕道而行。
verses.en: “In the days of Shamgar son of Anath,in the days of Jael caravans[NOTE:1] disappeared;[NOTE:2] travelers[NOTE:3] had to go on winding side roads.
notes: The translation assumes the form אֳרְחוֹת (ʾorekhot, “caravans”) rather than אֳרָחוֹת (ʾorakhot, “roadways”) because it makes a tighter parallel with “travelers” in the next line.
Or “ceased.”
Heb “Ones walking on paths.”

verses.zh: 以色列中的官长停职，直到我底波拉兴起，等我兴起作以色列的母。
verses.en: Warriors[NOTE:1] were scarce;[NOTE:2] they were scarce in Israel,until you[NOTE:3] arose, Deborah,until you arose as a motherly protector[NOTE:4] in Israel.
notes: The meaning of the Hebrew noun פְרָזוֹן (ferazon) is uncertain. Some understand the meaning as “leaders” or “those living in rural areas.” The singular noun appears to be collective (note the accompanying plural verb). For various options see B. Lindars, Judges 1-5, 237-38.
Or “ceased.”

The translation assumes that the verb is an archaic second feminine singular form. Though Deborah is named as one of the composers of the song (v. 1), she is also addressed within it (v. 12). Many take the verb as first person singular, “I arose” (cf. NAB, NASB, NIV).

Heb “mother.” The translation assumes that the image portrays Deborah as a protector of the people. It is possible that the metaphor points to her prophetic role. Just as a male prophet could be called “father,” so Deborah, a prophetess, is called “mother” (B. Lindars, Judges 1-5, 239).

verses.zh: 以色列人选择新神，争战的事就临到城门。那时，以色列四万人中岂能见盾牌枪矛呢？
verses.en: God chose new leaders,[NOTE:1] then fighters appeared in the city gates;[NOTE:2] but, I swear, not a shield or spear could be found[NOTE:3] among 40 military units[NOTE:4] in Israel.
notes: Or “warriors.” The Hebrew text reads literally, “He chose God/gods new.” Some take “Israel” as the subject of the verb, “gods” as object, and “new” as an adjective modifying “gods.” This yields the translation, “(Israel) chose new gods.” In this case idolatry is the cause of the trouble alluded to in the context. The present translation takes “God” as subject of the verb and “new” as substantival, referring to the new leaders raised up by God (see v. 9a). For a survey of opinions and a defense of the present translation, see B. Lindars, Judges 1-5, 239-40.

The translation of this difficult line is speculative because the second word, לָחֶם (lakhem), appears only here. The line in the Hebrew text literally reads, “Then [?] gates.” Interpretations and emendations of the Hebrew text abound (see B. Lindars, Judges 1-5, 239-40). The translation assumes a repointing of the form as a Qal participle לֹחֵם (lokhem) from the verbal root לָחַם (lakham, “fight”) and understands a substantival use (“fighter”). “Fighter” is a collective reference to the military leaders or warriors mentioned in the preceding line and in v. 9. (For other occurrences of the Qal of לָחַם, see Pss 35:1; 56:2-3.)
Heb “A shield, it could not be seen, nor a spear.” The translation assumes that the Hebrew particle אִם (ʾim) introduces an oath of denial (see GKC 472 §149.e).
Traditionally “40 thousand,” but this may be an instance where Hebrew term אֶלֶף (ʾelef) refers to a military unit. This is the view assumed by the translation (“40 military units”).

verses.zh: 我心倾向以色列的首领，他们在民中甘心牺牲自己。你们应当颂赞耶和华！
verses.en: My heart went out[NOTE:1] to Israel’s leaders,to the people who answered the call to war. Praise the Lord!
notes: The words “went out” are supplied in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 骑白驴的、坐绣花毯子的、行路的，你们都当传扬！
verses.en: “You who ride on light-colored female donkeys,who sit on saddle blankets,[NOTE:1] you who walk on the road, pay attention!
notes: The meaning of the Hebrew word מִדִּין (middin, “saddle blankets”) in this context is uncertain.

verses.zh: 在远离弓箭响声打水之处，人必述说耶和华公义的作为，就是他治理以色列公义的作为。那时耶和华的民下到城门。
verses.en: Hear[NOTE:1] the sound of those who divide the sheep[NOTE:2] among the watering places;there they tell of[NOTE:3] the Lord’s victorious deeds,the victorious deeds of his warriors[NOTE:4] in Israel.Then the Lord’s people went down to the city gates—
notes: The word “Hear” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.
The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain. Some translate “those who distribute the water” (HALOT 344 s.v. חצץ pi). For other options see B. Lindars, Judges 1-5, 246-47.
Or perhaps “repeat.”
See the note on the term “warriors” in v. 7.

verses.zh: 底波拉啊，兴起！兴起！你当兴起，兴起，唱歌。亚比挪庵的儿子巴拉啊，你当奋兴，掳掠你的敌人。
verses.en: “Wake up, wake up, Deborah!Wake up, wake up, sing a song!Get up, Barak!Capture your prisoners of war,[NOTE:1] son of Abinoam!
notes: Heb “take captive your captives.” (The Hebrew text uses a cognate accusative here.)

verses.zh: 那时有余剩的贵胄和百姓一同下来；耶和华降临，为我攻击勇士。
verses.en: Then the survivors[NOTE:1] came down[NOTE:2] to the mighty ones;[NOTE:3] the Lord’s people came down to me[NOTE:4] as[NOTE:5] warriors.
notes: This probably refers to those who responded to the call for war. They were “survivors” of the Canaanite oppression (see B. Lindars, Judges 1-5, 250).

The translation assumes a repointing of the verb as a perfect or imperfect/preterite form of יָרַד (yarad, “to go down”). The form as pointed in the MT appears to be from רָדָה (radah, “to rule”). See GKC 188 §69.g. The same form, translated “came down,” occurs in the next line as well.
The expression mighty ones probably refers to the leaders of the army.
The speaker may be Deborah here.
The translation assumes the preposition ב (bet) prefixed to “warriors” has the force of “in the capacity of.” For this use of the preposition, see GKC 379 §119.i.

verses.zh: 有根本在亚玛力人的地，从以法莲下来的；便雅悯在民中跟随你。有掌权的从玛吉下来；有持杖检点民数的从西布伦下来；
verses.en: They came from Ephraim, who uprooted Amalek;[NOTE:1] they follow[NOTE:2] after you, Benjamin, with your soldiers.From Makir leaders came down,from Zebulun came[NOTE:3] the ones who march carrying[NOTE:4] an officer’s staff.
notes: Heb “From Ephraim their root in Amalek” (the words “they came” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons). Because of the difficulty of the MT, many prefer to follow one of the ancient versions or emend the text. For various proposals see B. Lindars, Judges 1-5, 252-53. The present translation repoints שָׁרְשָׁם (shorsham, traditionally translated “their root”) as a Piel verb form with enclitic mem (ם). The preposition ב (bet) on עֲמָלֵק (ʿamaleq) introduces the object (see Job 31:12 for an example of the construction). Ephraim’s territory encompassed the hill country of the Amalekites (Judg 12:15).
The words “They follow” are supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.
The word “came” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.
Or possibly “who carry.”

verses.zh: 以萨迦的首领与底波拉同来；以萨迦怎样，巴拉也怎样。众人都跟随巴拉冲下平原；在流便的溪水旁有心中定大志的。
verses.en: Issachar’s leaders were with Deborah;the men of Issachar[NOTE:1] supported[NOTE:2] Barak;into the valley they were sent under Barak’s command.[NOTE:3] Among the clans of Reuben there was intense[NOTE:4] heart searching.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “Issachar.” The words “the men of” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Or “were true to.”
Heb “at his feet.”
Heb “great was.”
The great majority of Hebrew mss have “resolves of heart,” but a few mss read “searchings of heart,” which is preferable in light of v. 16.

verses.zh: 你为何坐在羊圈内听群中吹笛的声音呢？在流便的溪水旁有心中设大谋的。
verses.en: Why do you remain among the sheepfolds,[NOTE:1] listening to the shepherds playing their pipes[NOTE:2] for their flocks?[NOTE:3] As for the clans of Reuben—there was intense searching of heart.
notes: The meaning of the Hebrew word מִשְׁפְּתַיִם (mishpetayim) is uncertain. Some understand the word to mean “campfires.”
Or “whistling.”
Heb “listening to the pipe playing for the flocks.”

verses.zh: 基列人安居在约旦河外。但人为何等在船上？亚设人在海口静坐，在港口安居。
verses.en: Gilead stayed put[NOTE:1] beyond the Jordan River.As for Dan—why did he seek temporary employment in the shipyards?[NOTE:2] Asher remained[NOTE:3] on the seacoast;he stayed[NOTE:4] by his harbors.[NOTE:5]
notes: Apparently the people of Gilead remained on the other side of the river and did not participate in the battle.tn Heb “lived” or “settled down.”

Heb “Dan, why did he live as a resident alien, ships.” The verb גּוּר (gur) usually refers to taking up residence outside one’s native land. Perhaps the Danites, rather than rallying to Barak, were content to move to the Mediterranean coast and work in the shipyards. For further discussion, see B. Lindars, Judges 1-5, 262.
Heb “lived.”
Heb “lived” or “settled down.”
The meaning of the Hebrew word מִפְרָץ (mifrats) is uncertain, but the parallelism (note “seacoast”) suggests “harbors.”

verses.zh: 西布伦人是拚命敢死的；拿弗他利人在田野的高处也是如此。
verses.en: The men of Zebulun were not concerned about their lives;[NOTE:1] Naphtali charged onto the battlefields.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Zebulun was a people which despised its life even unto death.”
Heb “Naphtali was on the heights of the field.”

verses.zh: 君王都来争战。那时迦南诸王在米吉多水旁的他纳争战，却未得掳掠银钱。
verses.en: “Kings came, they fought;the kings of Canaan foughtat Taanach by the waters of Megiddo,[NOTE:1] but[NOTE:2] they took no silver as plunder.
notes: For location see Map1-D4; Map2-C1; Map4-C2; Map5-F2; Map7-B1.
The contrastive conjunction “but” is interpretive.

verses.zh: 星宿从天上争战，从其轨道攻击西西拉。
verses.en: From the sky[NOTE:1] the stars[NOTE:2] fought,from their paths in the heavens[NOTE:3] they fought against Sisera.
notes: Or “from heaven.” The Hebrew term שָׁמַיִם (shamayim) may be translated “heaven(s)” or “sky” depending on the context.

The MT takes “the stars” with what follows rather than with the first colon of v. 20. But for metrical reasons it seems better to move the atnakh (colon divider) and read the colon as indicated in the translation.
The words “in the heavens” are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied for clarity and for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 基顺古河把敌人冲没；我的灵啊，应当努力前行。
verses.en: The Kishon River carried them off;the river confronted them[NOTE:1]—the Kishon River.Step on the necks of the strong![NOTE:2]
notes: Possibly “the ancient river,” but it seems preferable in light of the parallel line (which has a verb) to emend the word (attested only here) to a verb (קָדַם, qadam) with pronominal object suffix.

This line is traditionally taken as the poet-warrior’s self-exhortation, “March on, my soul, in strength!” The present translation (a) takes the verb (a second feminine singular form) as addressed to Deborah (cf. v. 12), (b) understands נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) in its well-attested sense of “throat; neck” (cf. Jonah 2:6), (c) takes the final yod (י) on נַפְשִׁי (nafshi) as an archaic construct indicator (rather than a suffix), and (d) interprets עֹז (ʿoz, “strength”) as an attributive genitive (literally, “necks of strength,” i.e., “strong necks”). For fuller discussion and various proposals, see B. Lindars, Judges 1-5, 270-71.

verses.zh: 那时壮马驰驱，踢跳，奔腾。
verses.en: “The horses’[NOTE:1] hooves pounded the ground;[NOTE:2] the stallions galloped madly.[NOTE:3]
notes: The MT as it stands has a singular noun, but if one moves the prefixed mem (מ) from the beginning of the next word to the end of סוּס (sus), the expected plural form is achieved. Another possibility is to understand an error of scribal haplography here, in which case the letter mem should appear in both places.
The words “the ground” are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “galloped, galloped.” The repetition is for emphasis and is more appropriately indicated in English with an adverb.

verses.zh: 耶和华的使者说：应当咒诅米罗斯，大大咒诅其中的居民；因为他们不来帮助耶和华，不来帮助耶和华攻击勇士。
verses.en: ‘Call judgment down on[NOTE:1] Meroz,’ says the angel of the Lord;‘Be sure[NOTE:2] to call judgment down on[NOTE:3] those who live there,because they did not come to help in the Lord’s battle,[NOTE:4] to help in the Lord’s battle against the warriors.’[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “Curse Meroz.”
Heb “Curse, cursing.” The Hebrew construction is emphatic.
Heb “[to] curse.”
Heb “to the help of the Lord” (the same Hebrew phrase occurs in the following line). Another option is to read “to aid the Lord’s cause.”
Or “along with the other warriors.”

verses.zh: 愿基尼人希百的妻雅亿比众妇人多得福气，比住帐棚的妇人更蒙福祉。
verses.en: “The most rewarded[NOTE:1] of women should be Jael,the wife of Heber the Kenite!She should be the most rewarded of women who live in tents.
notes: Or “blessed.”

verses.zh: 西西拉求水，雅亿给他奶子，用宝贵的盘子给他奶油。
verses.en: He asked for water,and she gave him milk;in a bowl fit for a king,[NOTE:1] she served him curds.
notes: Or “for mighty ones.”

verses.zh: 雅亿左手拿着帐棚的橛子，右手拿着匠人的锤子，击打西西拉，打伤他的头，把他的鬓角打破穿通。
verses.en: Her left[NOTE:1] hand reached for the tent peg,her right hand for the workmen’s hammer.She ‘hammered’[NOTE:2] Sisera,she shattered his skull,[NOTE:3] she smashed his head,[NOTE:4] she drove the tent peg through his temple.[NOTE:5]
notes: The adjective “left” is interpretive, based on the context. Note that the next line pictures Jael holding the hammer with her right hand.
The verb used here is from the same root as the noun “hammer” in the preceding line.
Or “head.”
The phrase “his head” (an implied direct object) is supplied in the translation for clarification.
Heb “she pierced his temple.”

verses.zh: 西西拉在她脚前曲身仆倒，在她脚前曲身倒卧；在那里曲身，就在那里死亡。
verses.en: Between her feet he collapsed,he fell limp and was lifeless;[NOTE:1] between her feet he collapsed and fell, in the spot where he collapsed,there he fell—violently killed![NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and he lay.
Or “dead.”

verses.zh: 西西拉的母亲从窗户里往外观看，从窗棂中呼叫说：他的战车为何耽延不来呢？他的车轮为何行得慢呢？
verses.en: “Through the window she looked;Sisera’s mother cried out through the lattice:‘Why is his chariot so slow to return?Why are the hoofbeats of his chariot horses[NOTE:1] delayed?’
notes: Heb “chariots.”

verses.zh: 聪明的宫女安慰她（原文是回答她），她也自言自语地说：
verses.en: The wisest of her ladies[NOTE:1] answer;indeed she even thinks to herself,
notes: Or “princesses.”

verses.zh: 他们莫非得财而分？每人得了一两个女子？西西拉得了彩衣为掳物，得绣花的彩衣为掠物。这彩衣两面绣花，乃是披在被掳之人颈项上的。
verses.en: ‘No doubt they are gathering and dividing the plunder[NOTE:1]—a girl or two for each man to rape![NOTE:2] Sisera is grabbing up colorful cloth,[NOTE:3] he is grabbing up colorful embroidered cloth,[NOTE:4] two pieces of colorful embroidered cloth,for the neck of the plunderer!’[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “Are they not finding, dividing the plunder?”

Heb “a womb or two for each man.” The words “to rape” are interpretive. The Hebrew noun translated “girl” means literally “womb” (BDB 933 s.v. I. רַחַם), but in this context may refer by extension to the female genitalia. In this case the obscene language of Sisera’s mother alludes to the sexual brutality which typified the aftermath of battle.
Heb “the plunder of dyed cloth is for Sisera.”
Heb “the plunder of embroidered cloth.”
The translation assumes an emendation of the noun (“plunder”) to a participle, “plunderer.”

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，愿你的仇敌都这样灭亡！愿爱你的人如日头出现，光辉烈烈！这样，国中太平四十年。
verses.en: “May all your enemies perish like this, O Lord!But may those who love you shinelike the rising sun at its brightest.”[NOTE:1] And the land had rest for forty years.
notes: Heb “But may those who love him be like the going forth of the sun in its strength.”
